In practice

What it looks like when dates start to hold

What happened in the teams I was part of, measured before and after. The services are made from this work.

Real estate marketplace · CIB Vlaanderen · First product hire

Spotto

A plan I wouldn't promise landed a week early. The forecast would have said 86%.

86%
what a forecast would have said

The promise I wouldn't make

Two months after Spotto launched, the team was me and one developer. I was asked to commit to the plan for the quarter: 14 items by 30 June, with at most 10% left undone. I said I couldn't promise it. I had no number to go on, only a feeling that a team that small was too unsteady for a promise that tight.

13 of the 14 were accepted by 22 June, eight days early.

Three years later I ran a forecast on that team's own record, as it stood on the day I was asked. The plan had an 86% chance of holding. The number I needed was already sitting in our tracking history.

People expect a forecast to bring bad news. This one would have let me say yes. The Delivery Scan runs the same kind of forecast on your team's history.

Where the team came from

CIB, the federation of Belgian real estate agents, had tried to build this platform before. This time a launch date was set. In the months before launch, everyone was busy and nothing stayed finished. Every time the developers handed work over for review or testing, it came back 6 times in 10.

One list, one place for questions

The developers were emailing questions to the business side and waiting days for answers. I joined their Slack and became the first stop for every question and bug report. Answers went from days to minutes, and the developers got one list in one order.

"Done" meant one thing

I wrote the acceptance tests down: scenarios for each type of user, with a worked example of useful feedback. I tested releases myself. When one wasn't good enough the evening before it was due, I held it back.

A plan we checked every week

After launch I planned one quarter at a time, as a short list, and checked progress every week or two. When an urgent request for a feature came in, we gave a date six weeks out and named what would be dropped to make room. It shipped a day early.

I went back to the tracking history and measured three periods: before launch, around it, and the months after. A Delivery Realign takes the same measurement at the start, in the middle and at the end.

61% → 24% → 21% Hand-overs that came back after review or testing
23 → 16 → 11 days Within which 85% of the work was accepted

Not because the team grew. It shrank. Far less finished work came back, and the plan became something we checked every week instead of something we defended at the end.

When the team could be counted on, the attention went to what users needed. The platform grew from 10,000 to over 200,000 monthly visitors in two years.

Software company · ~12 people · Bootstrapped · Ghent · Agile coach on the team

Factry

18 months → 6
client implementation time

The situation

Factry builds software that runs on factory floors. Their previous client implementation had taken 18 months and nearly broke the team. A new client was coming. The technology wasn't the problem. How decisions were made and how work moved through the team was.

On the factory floor

I sat with the machine operators who would use the system, built rough prototypes and walked them back through those same operators before a line of production code was written. That removed weeks of rework.

In the team

The daily meeting had become an hour-long conversation between one developer and the founder while seven people waited. We took the founder out of it. Five one-hour meetings a week became fifteen minutes each.

The result

The next comparable client implementation took 6 months. Not because of a new framework or tool. Decisions happened faster, the right people were involved at the right time, and the team stopped waiting.

The number is already in your tracker.

Mine sat there for three years before I looked. Yours takes three minutes.
